routes.description: Establish that the West’s transformation toward universal concern is genuine moral progress by distinguishing changing applications from enduring moral principles and arguing that obligations, human dignity, moral comparison, and guilt require an objective standard grounded beyond evolved preference.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if shared moral principles and the normative features of obligation, progress, condemnation, and guilt are shown to require a mind-independent standard, and if Jesus’s expansion of concern is coherently explained as fuller recognition or application of that standard.

motionBridge.description: Show that Jesus’s historically transformative teaching points to genuine moral truth and progress rather than merely a change in prevailing inclination.

centralBridges.description: Distinguish enduring cross-cultural moral principles from historically variable practices and expansions of their scope.
Explain why obligations and rankings among conflicting inclinations require authority beyond contingently evolved feelings or preferences.
Connect objective human value and moral duties to grounding beyond humanity, including the account of persons as bearing God’s image.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend access to immaterial moral truth by distinguishing moral inquiry from the methods appropriate to physical science and history.
Use guilt and the perceived need for forgiveness as phenomena requiring comparison between realist and inclination-based explanations.

routes.description: Explain Western moral transformation as Jesus’s historically distinctive universalization of evolved and socially inherited concern, while arguing that human moral judgment, motivation, and practice can be grounded in constitutive inclinations without accessible objective values or divine grounding.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if historical variation and subjective epistemic access undercut the inference to objective morality, while evolved human nature and historically developed commitments adequately explain moral conviction, action, guilt, and the emergence of universal charity.

motionBridge.description: Show that Jesus’s influence can explain a major historical change in Western moral inclination without establishing objective or divinely grounded moral truth.

centralBridges.description: Establish that universal concern for unrelated needy people emerged historically and was not a constant feature of human moral practice.
Show how deeply rooted human nature and evolved inclinations can ground moral belief, motivation, and action without an external standard.
Explain why cognition through subjective human minds and persistent moral diversity limit any claimed access to objective moral values.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Provide evolutionary accounts of altruistic dispositions and guilt that do not presuppose a real moral code.
Separate the historical account of Jesus’s ethical influence from the further metaethical claim that the resulting values are objective.

sections.title: Objective Truth and Human Access
sections.rationale: The debate requires both sides to address whether mind-independent moral truth can exist and be known despite every judgment being formed through human cognitive faculties.

sections.title: Cross-Cultural Commonality and Historical Variation
sections.rationale: Claims about shared principles and divergent practices determine whether the historical record supports enduring moral truth or historically contingent human morality.

sections.title: Jesus and the Universalization of Charity
sections.rationale: The scope and meaning of Jesus’s extension of care beyond kin and social groups connects the agreed historical transformation directly to the competing explanations named in the motion.

sections.title: Inclination, Obligation, and Moral Progress
sections.rationale: The central normative clash is whether evolved inclinations can ground duties and comparisons among competing impulses or whether genuine obligation and progress require an objective standard.

sections.title: Guilt, Moral Practice, and Explanatory Scope
sections.rationale: Competing explanations of guilt, moral action, condemnation, and the transformation itself test how much each account explains beyond the historical facts both sides substantially accept.
